utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon, everyone in this courtroom. Good afternoon, General Galic. Although I do understand that the circumstances for you might have been very difficult, I nevertheless hope that you enjoyed the days that are behind us now, Christmas day and new year, and I wish you of course also with full understanding for the problems of especially General Galic, to wish you all the best for the coming year. Before resuming the cross-examination of Mr. Nakas, I would just like to see where we stand on a few issues. The first issue is that on December 6th, the Chamber has invited the Prosecution to provide further information regarding your request for protective measures for some witnesses, three of them. Chamber has not received any further information, so at this moment we'll just sit back and see what happens. The second issue is that a motion of the 30th of October, 2001 for a witness for whom a pseudonym was requested the motion was granted as far as the pseudonym was concerned, but no decision has been made on any further request in that respect, and we have no further -- we have not received any further information on that. I'd just complete first. Then the third issue I would like to draw your attention to, and I'm especially addressing the Defence, is that on the 10th of December, the Chamber has provisionally admitted the following Prosecution documents: 1601, 3369, 3369-1, 2794, 2795, 2506, 2183, 2795, 3573, 3573-1, 2265, 2272, and 2272-1. These were the medical records. They have been provisionally admitted. I would invite the Defence, if there are any objections, to raise them not later than today. Unless there are any specific remarks to be made on what I've just said -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic, you would like to make a remark on this? Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me the floor. As regards to the objection of the Defence on the medical documentation which has been provisionally admitted in a decision of the Chamber, concerns the authenticity of the documents. The documents in question are photocopies, and the Defence believes that without access to original documents, we are not in a position to accept the documents as being authentic. In particular, due to the fact that the identity of the documents has not been verified by the authorities in charge. According to the words of Mr. Nakas, the documents were authenticated only through a stamp of the hospital. During his examination, he testified that the documents in question can be found in their original form in the hospital's archives and that by looking at the stamp, he was able to confirm that the copies were consistent with the originals. The verification of the documents, that is, of the copies of the documents, in the area of the former Yugoslavia, and I believe that to be the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, is something that is the responsibility of a relevant municipal body or a relevant court. For these reasons, the medical documentation, which is, among other things, illegible, which have not been verified by the relevant authority cannot be accepted as authentic, because some of the documents have not been compiled on requested forms and they have not been confirmed with the signature of the physician. I have informed my learned colleagues of this problem in a letter, informing them that we would be challenging the authenticity of the medical documentation and we reserve our right to state our position as regards the authenticity of the documents only after a comparison has been made with the original documents and only after an expert analysis has been conducted by using adequate methods, graphological methods and chemical analysis methods as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. You'll understand that the Chamber has to consider your objection. I don't think it has to be done right away, since the examination-in-chief has been concluded by now, but we'll consider the objection and the admission is still provisional, as it was before. From the Prosecution side, is there any remark to be made concerning the issues I've raised a couple of minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon. I apologise if my voice gives a little trouble today. I've contracted something of a cold, so it may fade or sound rougher than normal, but I apologise for that. Your Honours, as regards the first issues you raised, namely the protective measures to be sought for witnesses, we have in fact prepared a motion which is ready to be filed. The reason we have waited this long is simply that the last of the witnesses of whom we had to make further inquiry could only be seen this very weekend in Sarajevo, and I received the necessary information for Your Honours yesterday, and it's been drafted and will be filed as soon as physically possible when we've concluded these court proceedings, which will be first thing tomorrow morning, I trust, Your Honours. The witnesses are not due to appear for a some little while, so I trust it causes you no problem. I don't know if you want any comment on the documentary issue at this stage, as you've taken on board my learned friend's objection in which to consider it. But I can address the issue if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just confer with my colleagues. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill. We'd like to hear your position as far as the objection concerning admission of the evidence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot off the cuff give you a line reference in the examination-in-chief of Dr. Nakas, but I do recall him giving evidence to the fact that he is something who is formally authorised to authenticate documents for his hospital. I recall him giving that evidence. I will certainly research it and back that up with a reference, although I believe my friend Mr. Ierace has found it. Yes. This is in fact page 1135 of the unofficial, non-corrected transcript, and at line 6 I asked the question: What was his authority in regard to issuing copies of reports and things at the request of patients or third parties? And he said, "Yes, at the request of a third party, I am authorised to be able to issue a copy of the report being requested on behalf of the hospital." And at that point the documentation was then in fact put to him for authentication. My learned friend has made certain references as to her position regarding supposed official channels that should be used to adduce documents, but I commend to you the evidence of Dr. Nakas. He has already stated he has authorised. The issue, as I understand it, is essentially this: If an authorised -- this is our position. If an authorised person can compare copies to original documents within their institution and is authorised then to say, "Yes, these are true copies," that is essentially the issue of authentication. From what I understand of my learned friend's point is that she seems to have more of an issue that it is something to do with the content of the document that would be in issue, or examination of the document in some forensic way. I don't see that that impacts upon the basic issue of authentication by an approved official of official documents. So that is a representation I would make. And beyond that, of course, equally, one would dispute, because we have nothing yet to indicate that this has to be so in law, that because a certain procedure of the former Yugoslavia as a central state was not followed, that does not mean that it would be improper or unacceptable or inadmissible if you receive evidence that another procedure is used, being the current procedure in the state and the institution from which the witness comes. I believe those would be the representations I put forward, Your Honour. I will just confer with my learned friend for a moment, if I may. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will leave my remarks to that, and I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you like to respond to the position of the Prosecution in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me invoke a case which was conducted before this Tribunal against the accused Vasiljevic, where the Chamber decided that all medical documents relied upon by the Defence, that is true, should be submitted to an expert for purposes of authentication. That is also one of the reasons -- one of the arguments in favour of our position. Only after that has been done we will state our position as regards the authenticity of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Any further observation from --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would only say, Your Honour, that I don't believe that that approach actually precludes Your Honours accepting the tender of documents as exhibits. It could be a matter that certain exhibits or leading from there certain inquiries need to be undertaken, but I don't believe that the issue of forensic investigation should preclude Your Honours from receiving into evidence documents in their own right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll just confer for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, my learned friend does remind me, of course, that there's also a matter of the vehicle through which exhibits are produced to the Court. There is a difference between certainly just a batch of documents being tendered, perhaps with no specific witness, but in this case we have the witness, who is available for cross-examination on this very issue, as well as other issues, and the responsible -- who has given evidence has being the responsible authority for the action. I think that may set it apart from the other case but I'm not certain as to the circumstances of the adducing of those particular records that my learned friend referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Then I think we are at a point where we could resume the cross-examination of Dr. Nakas. I would like to remind the Defence the specific rules on cross-examination, and it's the intention of this Chamber that at least a rule which is not in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence but which will be applied unless good cause is shown to act differently, that the time limit for cross-examination should be that it takes no more time than the examination-in-chief, and that's really a maximum. So it's not encouraging you to use the same time but at least not to exceed this time. And in that respect, I can tell you that the examination-in-chief -- I did write it down somewhere, but ... I'll check that. I've written it down, but I think you've spent until now 10 minutes on cross-examination. If the witness, please, could be brought in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakas, do you understand me -- do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then may remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made when you were examined in chief by the Prosecution, so you're still bound by that declaration. Please be seated. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakas, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of December, we began with the cross-examination, and on page 1156 of the transcript you stated that you had returned to the hospital on the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of function, what kind of position did you have at that time? You told us that you were an administrator. What kind of position is it, exactly?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, when the JNA left the former military hospital, I returned to the same hospital at around 10.00, and just like my other colleagues, who were still in the hospital and were working - there were about 40 of them at that time, together with the patients - and in view of the fact that most of them were involved in surgery, a group of people who were supposed to take control over the hospital thought that I should be the right person for leading the hospital until such a time when adequate position is defined by the then Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a member of the SDA at that time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I used to be a member of the Communist League in the former Yugoslavia up until 1990, and that was the end of my political involvement. I belonged to no political party as of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to investigators of the OTP, you stated that you had left the hospital on the 8th but that you had returned on the 10th of May. You also stated that you were well informed of everything that was taking place at the hospital through your brother, who was also an employee at the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did your brother ever tell you that during that period of time while you were absent during that month, the hospital was being targeted?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was no such information, but I did hear about the fact that the hospital had been targeted, had been hit at some point in time, but it was not my brother who told me that, but someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you that oxygen tanks were missing from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no mention of such a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in the hospital, how many patients were there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my memory serves me right, I believe that there were 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your subsequent work there, did this number of patients increase at any point in time or diminish?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, the former military hospital in Sarajevo had a very good reputation and it was one of the rare institutions which had a waiting list for patients who wanted to undergo surgery or treatment there. In the month of May, that documentation got lost and the majority of the patients who were either injured or ill were treated at the then clinical centre, medical/clinical centre in Sarajevo. So that at that time, up until the 10th of May, no patients were being brought to the former military hospital. However, after the 10th of May, we started admitting the victims who were brought there by either individuals, private individuals, or ambulances, so that after that date the number of patients increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you can recall: In 1992, what was the month or the period of the year when you had most patients, and what was the maximum of patients that you had that year?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the maximum of patients were admitted in 1993. That number was not so high in the summer of 1992. There was a certain increase during the winter, and the maximum patients we had in June 1993, when we had over 500 patients one particular month - I don't remember -- yes, in June. And I'm referring only to the injured, not other patients who came to the hospital for other purposes, and there were quite a few of them as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, what was the maximum number of patients at any point in time, up until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 150 and 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers among the patients that were admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were both civilians and soldiers who had been injured. It was an open-type hospital. We did not have any such restrictions. We were not specialised for either group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When a patient was admitted to your hospital, would this information always be supplied? That is, would you always note that he was either a civilian or a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last time I told you that the book of records were inherited from the former military hospital, which had appropriate forms and appropriate questions, such as whether the patient was a member of the military or a spouse or a member of the family, and that is why we continued supplying the same type of information. And we classified our patients in terms of their insurance, that is, whether they had a civilian type of insurance or a military type of insurance, but not according to the type of injury. That is, we would not specifically state whether they had been injured in combat or while going about their usual daily activities. So that information was done according to the type of insurance that they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And it was for the purposes of getting adequate compensation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the former system, we also had civilian patients in respect of whom we could claim money from the insurance company, but this was the type of information that we entered in our book of records, without actually expecting that we would be able to claim money for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you took the case history of the patients, would you, during that conversation, make a note of the location where they had been injured and the way in which they had been injured?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the work load and the shortage of personnel, both professional staff members or paramedics, the system of administration and the extent of medical data was reduced, and that is why we only compiled the most important data, the most relevant information for the type of injury or illness, and anything that would be relevant for the individual patient's condition: Sensitivity to certain drugs, allergies, and similar type of information. Very often the patients admitted to the hospital were not able to provide any such information, so such information was gathered from their escort, or whoever had brought them there. If that was not possible, then all we had was what we were able to establish objectively speaking, what we were able to actually see. In cases where we were able to compile information regarding the location of injuring and the type of injuring, we would enter that information as well. However, there was no particular requirement to supply that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you had various types of injuries and the fact that you always took information concerning the case history, did you report such cases further on?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the overall situation, we did not submit such reports. We did not have any particular obligation to supply relevant information except for the actual number of patients admitted to the hospital, which we forwarded to the relevant authorities. However, no official report was made on specific details. It concerned merely the number of patients who were treated on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you supplied the information about the number of injured persons to the Republican Committee. What was the actual function of that committee and what was the relevant period of time when you reported such cases?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republican Committee for health was established prior to April 1992. I believe that that institution was set up in 1992 because of the events in Croatia and because of the need to send out medical supplies. In the following period, this institution was a kind of coordinating body between the relevant medical authorities and institutions at the level of the Republic. However, at the time of the Sarajevo siege, most of the information which was supplied to that institution came from Sarajevo. The information was supplied on a daily basis by the local hospitals, and that information was further processed by this Republican Committee, which then produced relevant medical documentation which was published by the Republic Institute for Health. At the same time, this institution was in charge of supplying the UNHCR and other international organisations about the overall situation, and that data served as some kind of criteria for the distribution of medical aid to the institutions which were in greater need because they had many more patients or because their patients were mainly civilians, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of December, you were presented with documentation during the cross-examination, the documentation that you yourself have supplied, and you stated that your stamp was there to prove that these copies which were submitted to the Court are authentic to the originals and that the original documentation is kept, if my memory serves me right, at the hospital. I would like to know whether the documents produced and looked at as evidence -- well, do you believe that this is full and complete documentation relating to the full case history?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the documents that I recognised in the month of December as documents photocopied, dully photocopied and the originals of which are to be found at the General Hospital of Sarajevo is a cross-section of documentation compiled during that period, and that includes all the various forms pertaining to the case history, temperature charts, specialist papers, and everything else. I'm of the view that between 1992 and 1995, the administration was somewhat reduced, it was carried out on a reduced scale, and this means that there are some shortcomings when it comes to these documents, but considering the time that we had and the space we had, that was the best we could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what the case history includes and whether everybody single patient will have a separate case history?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the case history is an official document which lists personal data of the insured person admitted to the hospital. On the front we have the name, surname, date and place of birth, the type of insurance, the telephone number in case of need, the cause, the diagnosis, the date of admission, date of release from hospital, the diagnosis, procedures engaged in by the hospital and recommendation referring to any further treatment after the release from the hospital. Also on the front page of this case history document there are the signatures of the doctors and there are also boxes which up until 1992 were used to indicate special codes for case histories according to the Belgrade system. On the second page we have a blank page. We've got a case history there. And either manually or on a typewriter you enter the data, with reference to any data provided by either the patient himself or the accompanying persons, any previous illnesses suffered by the patient, and then an objective diagnosis which traditionally followed a traditional procedure which would refer to the general state of health, the description of the skin and all the various other body parts, and in the period of time between 1992 and 1995, we've simply reduced this to include a specific diagnosis, that is to say, the reason for which the patient was admitted to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise if I've been a bit long-winded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Doctor. Who is in charge of filling out those forms?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front page is filled out by the medical technician, the administrator, a member of the administrative staff working at the admissions office. As to the case history, on the inside of this paper pertaining to the purely medical information it is filled out by the doctor who first treated or saw the patient when the patient was first admitted. And as to the last page, the conclusions, that is, it is filled out by the patient releasing -- by the doctor releasing the patient from the hospital. And then he fills out the data pertaining to the final diagnosis. So as I was saying, first of all the administrative staff and then the medical bit is filled out by the doctors, only and exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does every patient have his own case history?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every patient admitted to the hospital has a special registration number and a case history which is evidence and the records are kept at the specific ward where the patient spends time. For other patients, we have the data which are kept in the book of records, and once a year it is all put in the same book of records. As to the day hospital treatment, the medical technicians are in charge of filling out the data, that is to say, names and surnames, the age, the insurance policy, et cetera, and the diagnosis is filled out either by the doctor or else the doctor dictates it to another member of staff if he's working and is unable to write at the same time. But generally speaking, as to the diagnosis, the treatment, and the recommendations for the papers, all that is filled out by the doctor examining the patient, and if not possible, then the medical technician will do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to submit to you the documents that you have already had the opportunity to look at. Once you've perused it again, I would like you to answer the following question: Do you believe that this represents the complete documentation for the persons, these people admitted to your hospital whilst keeping in mind everything that you have just said in the course of this conversation between the two of us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document you are now showing to the witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I suggest that the Court copy would perhaps be the appropriate one to be handed down to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with that, but in order to know -- to give the Court copy to the witness, we have to know what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not in a position to tell you exactly what number it is at the moment. Perhaps my colleagues will be able to help me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you have been provided with a list of exhibits, an updated list of the exhibits. That's what the Registry told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "P," if that's the one,"P2506". The number of the document is 00267861. In the upper corner, to the right, 25065. I also have 252265, 2265, presumably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I think that the first one is 2506, not 25065.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2506 plus 2265.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you have the documents in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one which is 2265, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether, in your view, this represents the complete set of documents and case history histories in line with the rules and procedures of your institution, the institution that you've headed? Do you feel that these documents are acceptable?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of these documents is a copy of the findings evidenced in the book of records of the emergency services of the General Hospital of Sarajevo, and the second part is a photocopy of the documents which were issued to patients which came for treatment at the day hospital over a certain period of time. This does not represent a case history. These are just specialist findings given to patients after reporting to the medical services, if, that is to say, they're not kept at the hospital. There are the numbers of the documents, names, the diagnosis, and the recommendations made to the patients, plus the signatures and the stamps of the doctors in charge. So basically, this is a copy of the original document, which is a specialist finding. These are complete documents but since this is not a case history here --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just specify what the protocol number is, the record number?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one is 775, in the left-hand corner, 775.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And for 7861, 7862, 7863, 7864, where we don't see any stamps?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any of those documents here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 863, 887, 876, 863, and the first one I think, since it is not all that clear, I think it is 775. Here on the screen I see it is indeed 775.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my numbers are completely different. The numbers submitted by my colleagues. 2265. Could we just compare this? These are the numbers of the pages. I wouldn't like really to read out the names of the people. Perhaps it might be easier, but I would prefer to read out the numbers. 52265. Let us confine ourselves to that. P2265. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The last digits, 464. I suppose that's going to be easier.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you're not referring to the record numbers. That's what you asked for, the hospital record numbers. That's what I had in mind. And this is the evidence number. Yes, I can repeat that. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. There's no need for that, Doctor. I'm just going to ask you whether you have your records back at the hospital, and apart from what we have here, do you have anything else within the framework of that book of records?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We only have the book of records.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And that book of records exists at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more point I'd like you to respond to. You have no case histories for any of these people who have these documents.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone receiving day hospital treatment have these kinds of documents. That means that basically, as far as they're concerned, everything is summed up in these findings. Now, if we refer to individual protocol numbers and we look at what happened to these people, we can see that some of them were indeed admitted to the hospital. For example, if you allow me, 268, 464, here the doctor says that the patient should be admitted, but the person was released on the 7th of February. Yes. The patient was admitted and we have a full case history at the hospital. Here we do not have a case history, just a specialist finding. If we look at the part dated the 5th of February, we do have a case history there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did say that you arrived at the hospital on the 10th of May. Upon your arrival, as far as you can tell, when was the first time that the hospital was shelled? You did say it was shelled.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was on the 13th of May, in the afternoon and in the evening. Obviously, this is etched in my mind, because this is the first shelling. The first one was on the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that once you arrived at the hospital, you put up a Red Cross flag and that it stayed there for about six to nine months?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photo. This is a photo which I obtained from the Prosecution, which the Defence obtained from the Prosecution. If you would be so kind as to take a look at it and tell us whether this is accurate and when this photo might have been taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to tender this into evidence, Ms. Pilipovic, this photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the witness recognises the picture and if he's in a position to give some sort of explanation, yes. That is to say in case the witness is able to identify the period of time when the picture was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at least it should be -- since you consider to tender it into evidence, have you prenumbered it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May we be made privy to the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I expected. You have not provided the Prosecution with a copy -- it comes from you, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least it might have been indicated that it was going to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I'm not doubting my learned friend's word. We just don't know what particular photo she is referring to at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this photo suitable for putting on the ELMO so that we can have a look at that in order to prevent any loss of time? Is this picture for the time being good enough, Mr. Blaxill, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly recognise what's depicted in there. We're quite happy with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nakas, can you see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the period of time when this photograph might have been taken?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, it must have been taken in summertime or in the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While this photograph is in front of you, would you tell us -- would you show us the floor where your offices were located and tell us about the direction they were facing.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the portion of the hospital which is depicted on the photograph, that is, the wing of the hospital where the patients were located --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I hesitate to interrupt, but I have a feeling we're not getting the full photograph on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the ELMO -- I don't see any photo at all any more on the screen, to be quite honest. Could there be any technical assistance in order to see whether the ELMO is functioning or not? Perhaps in the meantime the Prosecution could have a look at the photo in its entirety so that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I am indeed familiar with that photograph. Now I see it all, Your Honour. So there's no problem from that point of view. The ELMO seems to have gone blank on us again -- oh, because they've taken the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's my screen. It's ours. Now I've got it. I've got the photo again on my screen. I see my neighbour to the left as well. Has everyone the photo on the screen by now? Okay, then. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you tell us the location of your offices?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph we see the 12-storey building as the central part of the hospital compound, which was formerly used for the treatment of patients, this part here. This portion here was used for surgery purposes. As for the building where my office was located, and outpatient clinics, they're not visible on the photograph. They're to the right side of this building. This building is covering that portion of the compound. It is an apartment block. I think that the photograph was taken from the Albanska Street, which is now called Dolina Street, and on the right-hand side you can see a building which belongs to the Sarajevo-Stan company, which is covering a portion of this 12-storey building. But normally to the right you would see a two-storey building where my office was located. So one cannot see my offices here on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see the Magribija Dzamija from your office?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards my offices and other offices in this building, the Magribija Dzamija would have been easily seen, but it was destroyed sometime in 1992. But you could see it, because it is -- it dominates that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately the time when the mosque was blown up?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was hit by a shell in 1992, at the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, in May or June?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. At the beginning of 1992. By the end of 1992 it was destroyed. It was split in half.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the mosque, since your offices were facing the mosque, were there any incidents there that could have been related to the shelling? And as far as you can recall, were there any victims in those shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on two or three occasions we admitted patients from that area, from the Magribija mosque, and at one point in time, from this street, the Albanska Street, where you can see a car, a group of people was brought to the hospital, and I was really fortunate in the sense that I was able to observe those patients and the way they were brought to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you were able to see those individuals who were victims in this shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you keep any records of shelling incidents of the hospital itself and the area around it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards records of shelling, there were no specific records of the shelling incidents of the hospital and the area around it. We did not have adequate means to keep those records.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection, did you ever report such cases to relevant authorities, or was there an individual at the hospital who was in charge of reporting such cases to the relevant authorities, and did relevant authorities ever visit the scene to establish the damage and the consequences of the incident involving casualties?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict in June up until August 1992, we submitted some reports to the former centre for security of the town of Sarajevo. I'm not quite sure about the official title of this institution. So during the first several months somebody would come from time to time to make a record of the damage, but they did not keep any record of the number of patients or victims. However, later on, when it became a common occurrence, these shelling incidents, which would usually start at dawn, they no longer came and we no longer reported such incidents. It simply became our daily life.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the hospital ever visited by members of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital was handed over to the legal authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina by virtue of an agreement which had been signed by the representative of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the representative of the former JNA, UNPROFOR, and ICRC, with the caveat that the ICRC should take over the administration of the hospital. Unfortunately, the agreement was never fully implemented, because the ICRC abandoned the town of Sarajevo after a humanitarian convoy had been hit in the vicinity of Sarajevo and one of their drivers was killed. So for about seven or ten days, the Ministry of Health was in charge of organising the work of the hospital there, so they appointed the managing board of the hospital. And from then on we received regular visits of the members of UNPROFOR, which at the beginning, after we had been shelled for the first time, consisted in making appropriate records of the damage, which was caused, and later on, when the air lift was established, their visits mostly concerned the supply of medical aid or examination of patients which were to be evacuated from the hospital. But we also received visits of some high-ranking officials, such as the French president Mitterrand, who visited the hospital together with other dignitaries of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As regards members of UNPROFOR who had an opportunity to visit the hospital, did they ever make any reports or records concerning the situation in the hospital, and specifically, did they make any record, any note of the shelling of the hospital and where it came from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I think -- as far as I know, they kept such records for their own purposes, but the hospital never received any official reports or any official records that were compiled by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the existence of any observation point of the United Nations in the vicinity of the hospital and where it was located exactly?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the UN did not have a permanent observation point anywhere near the hospital; however, they patrolled the area, the streets around the hospital, and they observed the overall area where the hospital was located. However, they did not have any official observation point near the hospital except for the points that served as a shelter from snipers. But they had nothing to do with the hospital itself. In the agreement that I mentioned a moment ago, the UNPROFOR had the obligation to protect the hospital from possible incidents once the JNA has left the hospital. However, that type of protection given by UNPROFOR was never actually implemented. So the UNPROFOR only visited the hospital from time to time for the purposes of verifying the situation in the hospital, but they never offered any official protection to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that the UN members patrolled the area around the hospital. Do you have any knowledge whether they visited the scene when the hospital or the area around the hospital was shelled? Would they visit the scene officially upon receiving any special official report, and did they make any report following such visits?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they did visit the area from time to time and did make some records, but I never received any such official information. And we had a duty to receive members of UNPROFOR and the United Nations and to provide them with all the information that they would request, including the number of patients and their names, if necessary. And also, whenever they escorted patients evacuated from the hospital, they were involved in monitoring the situation in the hospital generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So can I therefore conclude that there were written reports following visits of the UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of such documents were compiled in the presence of the staff on duty at the emergency ward, but such documents were never shown to any member, any staff member of the hospital to be signed by them. Those documents were the property of UNPROFOR and we had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Whilst you were examined by my learned colleague on the 10th of December, you testified that it was from Trebevic and Vrace that the hospital was usually targeted.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the photograph in front of you, could you tell us -- could you confirm that the lower part of the hospital could be targeted from that area, from Vrace and Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, one can see that there is a kind of corridor or the street which used to be called Albanska Street but which is now called Doljanska Street. There was an open passage, so there was an opportunity to shell the hospital, the front part of the hospital. The left and right part of the hospital were better sheltered by surrounding buildings, but this part of the hospital compound was located at the end, or rather, at the beginning of the Albanska Street, and the view was not obstructed in any way from the area of Trebevic and Vrace. That is, the hospital could be directly seen from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you have some knowledge about weapons. You are probably in a position to tell us the type of weapons that the hospital was hit from.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of shell fragments that we were able to find in the hospital, one can conclude that the ammunition came from various tanks and other types of artillery and mortar pieces. As regards my knowledge of these things, I am better versed in small arms, pistols and automatic rifles. I must admit that I am not well versed in this type of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark on this photograph the portion of the hospital which was targeted by shells coming from a tank?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very difficult to do it here on this photograph. It is quite possible that the majority of these holes are the result of a shelling from a tank. I think that there was a tank shell which directly impacted the area on the 10th floor, but that's all I can tell about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the OTP, you also provided an analysis, a breakdown, of the number of civilians and military men who were admitted to the hospital from 1992 to 1995. According to you, the total was 8.105, out of which 3.698 were civilians and 4.407 soldiers. Is it your testimony that that would constitute a ratio of 50/50, civilians and military personnel?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be close to 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You compiled this information on the basis of your personal records?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the basis of the reports which were submitted to me through the emergency ward of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the medical documentation that we have here, could you perhaps tell us if the same documents can be found in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the official archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is only recently that we have received a request from the archives, but it's only a verbal request, not an official written request, that the medical documentation be transferred to the official historical archives. However, appropriate records thereof should be kept at the hospital. But all this relevant medical information relating to the war should be kept at the official state archives of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's only one set of such documents that has been handed over to the archives by the Dobrinja Hospital, which no longer exists, so that is how the documentation from the Dobrinja Hospital ended up in the state archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you stated that you are authorised to authenticate the documents coming from the hospital, pursuant to requests made by third parties.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who is in charge of authenticating copies of documents? Would it be you or the relevant authorities, such as court, or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am authorised to do so on behalf of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but are you also authorised to verify that the copy is consistent with the original?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because my signature can be found at the municipal court in Sarajevo. It has been deposited as such for the purposes of verifying the documents bearing my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you deposit that signature?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was deposited earlier on, at the beginning of my mandate, and then once again, recently, when I was re-elected, that is, last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Does one of the colleagues have any additional questions before giving an opportunity for -- no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, I've got one question for you. You told us about the insurance, either military or not military. If the military insurance would pay for the treatment of a patient, would this mean that the patient was a military or could it also be a dependent, wife, children? Could you please explain about that.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1992, in the National Health Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had two possible schemes. One was the civilian insurance system. There was a network of public hospitals to cover that. And the second one had to do with the military insurance, which meant full cover for all members of the JNA and family members. And in the course of that period of time, the armed forces had a separate system of primary health care at their unit's garrisons and they had special services for big garrisons and then they had military hospitals in large areas. It is in this way that the military budget paid for the health care of the people insured and then they possibly paid for services supplied by civilian hospitals in case the members of the military were sent there for treatment. At the same time, the civilian insurance system also used the services of the military hospitals, which then they had to pay for. We've continued with this automatic system for the case histories, et cetera, and we classified our patients as military personnel and civilians. And when we say "military," it meant their dependents as well. As to the actual payments, well, it was not considered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, I'm not that interested in the payment as such but merely to know whether registration is militarily insured also meant they were military men or also they could be dependents. Mr. Blaxill, is the Prosecution in need of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We did have re-examination on various issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Can you estimate how much time it will take and perhaps guide the witness a bit in coming to the most relevant areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At the time, Your Honour, I think a matter of minutes really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, referring to this question of the military insurance, firstly, was military insurance for medical service restricted only to serving members of JNA or would it cover retired members or people who had formerly served in some capacity and move on? Would their family still continue to get it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they're in the active service or retired, were covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And if, for instance, a patient would come into hospital who is clearly a civilian person who is the dependent of a military person, would you still enter up that person as covered by the military insurance?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what if -- pardon me. And so how big a family group was covered by that kind of insurance? Did it go only to the spouse, to the children, or to any other relatives of such a military person?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular cover referred to the insured person, the spouse, any dependent children, and all those living with them or supported by them, such as elderly parents or anyone else who is related to them and has no other medical insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On that basis, I have just one other issue I'd like to ask you about, and that is this: You gave the figures that on the basis of military insurance and civilian insurance it looked as though you had 50/50, military and civilian patients. But with those entries for military insurance, did that in fact, within those figures, include such dependents, civilian dependents like parents, children, spouses?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's all. I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Dr. Nakas, this concludes your testimony in this court. I thank you very much not just for coming but even for coming twice. We really deplore that you had to come back after a couple of weeks. We would have loved to conclude your testimony already in December, but it was for practical reasons impossible. So thank you very much for coming twice to The Hague. Mr. Usher, you may lead the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think this is the time when we have a break of approximately half an hour. So we'll resume at 4.15, unless there's any opposition against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's just one point. It's just a practical matter. In the course of his being seen prior to testifying later today, the next witness, Mr. Ashton, was shown a couple of segments from the video that was used by my learned friend, Mr. Ierace, at the opening of the case. For the Court's information, that is now marked as, if I remember correctly, MFI-8. Now, I would propose wishing to play those clips to Mr. Ashton later in the course of his evidence. I will imagine it will be tomorrow. I think logistically it would cause no interruption or problem if we make it tomorrow. And we will obviously arrange things to achieve that. But it isn't on the witness list or exhibit list per se, because in fact we didn't know until Mr. Ashton came in from the United States and could be seen and shown these clips of course whether this would be relevant to do this. It has become relevant. And so I put everyone on notice that we would like to do that, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said as the next witness -- Mr. Ashton being the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We have in fact been able to avoid calling the lady by the name of Kelma Muminovic. And I thought the Court had been notified. If you were unaware, then please accept an apology, Your Honours. We will be moving straight now to Mr. Ashton. We have advised the Defence, I would add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not aware of it, but perhaps I have overlooked something. Then, finally, before going on recess, we still have -- Ms. Pilipovic, you would like to say something, but I would also like to ask you what to do with the photograph, the photograph you showed to Dr. Nakas, because you said it depends on what he testifies, whether it should be either marked for identification or -- yes. Marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the numbering is in the hands of the registry, as far as the identification is concerned. So the prenumbering as a potential exhibit has fallen away now and the photograph is marked for identification. Thank you. Then we'll resume -- I beg your pardon. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just going to make a statement on behalf of the Defence with reference to the fact that my colleagues decided not to listen to the witness statement. I only found out yesterday, and I would really like to ask my colleagues to let us know on time, because I myself spent a great deal of time preparing that witness, and then they desisted from -- not to call the witness. So I do hope they will take account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm advised the information was given Monday after the decision was taken during the course of Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do agree with Ms. Pilipovic that these kind of messages should be delivered as soon as possible and practicable, and I have no reasons to believe at this moment that it has not been as soon as possible and as practical as possible, but let's try to avoid a waste of time for the other party and for the Court as well. Thank you. We'll resume for the fifth time, I think I say it now, at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that it will take us some time to get used to the practice I'm promoting in this courtroom. I'd just like to remind the Defence that their cross-examination took 70 minutes, where the examination-in-chief took 63 minutes, just seven minutes. But I'd like you -- I said that the maximum was the same time, unless good course was shown, so I just keep a close eye on the clock. Mr. Blaxill, is it you whose going to call on behalf of the Prosecution the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is indeed, Your Honour, yes. That's Mr. John Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. John Ashton. Would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. You have been called by the Prosecution as a witness in this case, and I'd first like to invite you, please, if you hear me in a language that you understand, but it might not be the main problem, to make the solemn declaration required by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The text is given to you by the usher. Would you please make the solemn declaration, raising your right hand, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm obliged to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, good afternoon. Would you please state for the record your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: My name is John Ashton, born September 30, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what in fact is your present occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I'm executive director of an international humanitarian agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: About with what does that particular agency concern itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Primarily medical distribution in disaster areas, conflict zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ashton, if I can take you back to: What was your family background? In what type of family did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I grew up in a military family, career navy. I grew up in an area where there was a naval surface weapon centre. My father worked there and my brothers were stationed in military bases around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would allow me, Mr. Blaxill. Mr. Ashton, would you please, with one eye at least, follow the transcript which is on the screen in front of you, because since you're speaking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a blue screen here. Now I have a black screen. There it is. Now the transcript just came up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpretation, since you're both speaking the same language, needs some time to translate the question first and then the answer. So if you would please wait every time until the question that has been put to you has appeared on the screen and then answer the question. Otherwise we might be in trouble. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, while you were a child growing up, did you take any particular interest in things military, or was that not of particular interest to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I had a very strong interest in the military. I studied weapons, weapon systems, aviation, primarily because I originally thought I would go into the military as a career, and I did choose a military career. I went into the civil coast guard service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When did you enter the coast guard service, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I entered the coast guard in 1973, upon graduation from high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I'm presuming by that you mean reference to the United States coast guard?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: United States coast guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how long did you serve with the United States coast guard?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I was with the coast guard for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did this duty for three years, did this take you to any other countries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Indeed. I went in during the Vietnam war, at which time I was trained to handle weaponry systems for the US military because the coast guard was handling the river patrols in Vietnam. So I had full military training at the time, studied Soviet weapon systems, had very extensive knowledge on military tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you said you served until 1976. What did you then do in 1976?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: When I left the coast guard I took a job as a photo journalist. I travelled to other areas to cover different situations. Actually, in 1976, I went to Beirut Lebanon as one of my first assignments for United Press International and covered the Lebanese civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you tell us any other such areas of conflict that you may have visited in your career and when you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. In -- later in 1977 I was in Eritrea. I travelled to Afghanistan in 1980 and 1981. I was working with the committee for Free Afghanistan in Washington, had the opportunity to go there and assist in getting aid to the Afghans during the Russian occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you remember any other places that you had been? Let us say prior to the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, I was in North Africa and other countries. I was in -- I've been to Somalija, I've been to Suedan, I've been to, as I mentioned, Eritrea. I was also in Morocco.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And as a photo journalist, did these assignments place you ever close to the actual realities of combat, of gunfire and the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: In every situation I was exposed to combat. My particular area of specialty is photograph conflict so I was on the front lines in several occasions, and on every occasions of these incidents I photographed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I could move forward, you've referred up to the early 1980s. After that did you pursue any other lines of work or photo journalism until, let us say, the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- well, in New York I was working as a photo journalist as well, and I did -- of course, I went to university to get some education and I took some courses in university. I did not complete university.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you advise what courses you took?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I took history, history of religion, political science and psychology courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you at any time, as a result of -- pardon me -- of pursuing any of in your careers, did you take any form of medical training?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I studied premed and trained at the National Institutes of Health in Washington. I worked in pediatric oncology for a brief time in the National Institutes of Health where I had extensive training in pharmaceuticals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let me take you please now, Mr. Ashton, to the year 1992. In the middle of that year, can you say where you went and what you were doing by way of a profession?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I was working in New York as a photographer and I was invited to come to Europe on assignment, and when I came to Europe I ran into someone who I had known from the Lebanese conflict in 1976 who was working for the United Nations, and he asked me to come to the former Yugoslavia for two weeks to take pictures for the United Nations, and I agreed to do it for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall when you actually arrived and in which place you actually came to, which city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I originally went to Zagreb, Croatia, met the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees staff. They arranged for me to go to Sarajevo on a UN flight out of Split, Croatia. This was July -- the first time was July 5th, 1992. And then I came out, after going in on that date, and came back on the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you then remain in Sarajevo for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I planned, as I said in my original statement, to stay for two days here, and what happened was I got trapped at the Sarajevo State Hospital due to heavy shelling. And when I went into the hospital I decided to take some pictures there of the conditions in the hospital. When I saw what was happening, I realised I was going to spend the night, so I started organising needs for that hospital while I was there and realised that I wasn't going to get out the next day either. But went down to the UN headquarters and they said they would arrange for me to leave, and I stayed again the next day to get those requests from the hospital for particular medical items that they were short of to the United Nations, at which time I decided to stay for two more weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did any event occur later in July of 1992 which caused you to leave the city of Sarajevo for a period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time I tried to arrange for a few things to be done, and I realised how complex the issues were, especially with the city being cut off from aid. At the airport only a small amount of aid was able to come in, so the hospital was very desperate. So I extended my stay a third week, and at the end of that time, July 23rd, I was out taking pictures with a group of Croatian and Bosnian friends of mine and got shot in the leg and shot in the arm by a sniper on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Firstly, I would ask you: Where in fact did that incident occur to you? Where did it happen? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The location was Otes, and I was shot from a railroad track on the edge of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how were you able to deduce the source of the shot that hit you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: We were able to cross the front lines and we were able to talk -- actually, it was very interesting. We were able to talk to some of the Serbs on the side. The Croatians and Bosnians I was walking with had relatives on the other side and at that point it had been relatively quiet. And we came across an area where there were some young men who knew the men I was with and the Serbs were talking to the Croats. Then we moved down to another location which was a railroad bridge, and at that position we had to cross a street and I was told by the forces I was walking with that this was very dangerous because these were former JNA soldiers at this particular area. I don't know how they knew that, but that's what I was told and that we would have to run across that street. And when we got into the street, four men in front of me went across and there were several behind me. There was no problems, so I didn't run very fast. And then I saw four men on the railroad track itself laying down. One of them got up, raised his gun up and fired one shot, which went across my face, and then he fired a second shot and I had started to run at that point and I fell, and I did not realise that was the shot that hit my leg. Then he fired a third shot which missed me by going over my head and hit the street behind me. Then a fourth shot when I pushed up off the ground to run and realised my leg was completely broken and shattered from the first shot -- from the second shot. At that point I was rescued by the other men behind me and pulled out of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've referred to the four men lying on the railroad track. Can you say what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: They were all wearing green uniforms. As best I could tell, the three that had gotten up high enough to look to see what was going on, the fourth man had gotten up completely to his waist, so I could see him quite clearly. But it all took place fairly quickly. It was within a matter of seconds. And at that point the team I was travelling with had time to get their weapons up and return fire, and then everyone went down behind the railroad bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you manage to see or indeed were you given any information that led to any further identification of the people who were on the railway lines, one of whom shot you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell what forces they came from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. Later, at a point later on, after I had returned from Germany and began working on the Serb side, one of the Serb commanders actually offered to introduce me to the man who shot at me, which I declined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you've just made reference to a Serb commander making this offer. Can you tell the Court in which military formation this man was a "Serb commander," the one who spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. He was with the Romanija Corps in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now the term "Romanija Corps" is that the full name of the unit -- military formation to your knowledge or does it have a longer name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, they call themselves the army of the Republic of Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And the name of that particular formation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Was the Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just the Romanija Corps. I see. So now when you were shot, you were with, you say, a group of people. Who were those people? What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: They were wearing -- two of them were wearing military uniforms. The rest were wearing civilian clothes. Five of them were actually policemen from the city of Bosnia -- from the city of Sarajevo. Correction. They escorted me out because one of them was a very good friend I had made there in the first weeks I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What were you wearing at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I was wearing blue jeans and a short-sleeved light-blue shirt. But I had cameras with me and I was told that at that point the publicity had become so bad for the opposing side, on the Serbian side, that they were actually getting paid 300 Deutschmarks to shoot journalists or anybody with cameras, and I didn't take that seriously, I guess, and found out the hard way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, you made reference to Germany. Did you in fact therefore leave Sarajevo as a result of your injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was flown out ten days later by the United States military on a aid flight which took me back to Rhein-Mein Germany and I was admitted to the US military hospital there, which could not treat my leg properly. So I went to Munich, to a private German hospital, where the doctors said they would like to have me to treat me for free. And while I was there, they heard about the situation in Bosnia and decided to help with medicines, to supply medicines to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And from receiving your treatment in Germany, did you then at some point return to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I returned on about the 22nd of August, somewhere in that area. I'm not sure exactly what date right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you remain in Sarajevo for the remainder of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I made a few weekend trips out on United Nations flights just to get away from the situation, from the airport there, and I returned to the airport the following Monday or Sunday evening, whenever I could get on a flight back in. But during the weekdays I was in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you take any other employment during the last few months of 1992 whilst you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
