utterances.text: Well, the situation was so bad in the hospitals there in Sarajevo and the medical clinics that UNHCR had asked me -- the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, to define UNHCR, had asked me to assist with making assessments because the World Health Organisation's offices had left Sarajevo early in the conflict, in April, and I began making assessments for the hospitals and turning those over to UNHCR. So UNHCR asked me if I would like to work for them, and in October 1991 I took a position with the UNHCR and became a member of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that employment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Until the end of November I was a little bit disappointed with the way humanitarian aid was being managed and decided to tried to work with the Germans that I had met in Germany to develop a humanitarian aid agency that would supply proprietary medicines that were not getting into the city, into the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you succeed in that ambition at any time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a problem getting it started. We finally got the organisation Emergency Medical Response Agency legal and set up in Germany on the beginning of March, 1993. In the interim, I just brought medicines in through the United Nations system, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and by then WHO had come back into the city, so I began working closely with them and the Ministry of Health in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, briefly, you had observed conditions earlier in 1992, in July, within the city of Sarajevo, and can you just very briefly tell the Court what was happening in that city when you arrived there in the July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: When I first arrived in July 1992, I was stunned by the amount of violence against civilians. I had been to several wars preceding this time, as stated in my previous testimony here, and this particular situation was very alarming because I had never seen so many civilian casualties in a short period of time, daily, coming into the hospitals and deliberately targeted. Most of the conflicts I had been in, there were civilian casualties, but nothing compared to this, because most of the conflicts were military forces fighting other military forces on front line positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now on that basis, may I take you to the question. You said, "these many civilian casualties." Did you witness the circumstances in which these -- a number of these people became casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I -- in fact, I took some risk to try to rescue people who were shot in front of me or who were wounded by shelling in front of me. I saw on several occasions, and of course I photographed incidents where people were wounded and killed in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And taking account of your various experiences which you've already informed the Court of, did you take any steps to try and ascertain where some of these sources of fire were, be they, you say by shelling or people shot by bullets? Did you do anything of that type?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, and I was -- when I was in the Holiday Inn the first month I arrived, I stayed at the Holiday Inn until I was wounded, and from there was a Canadian contingent from UNPROFOR, from the United Nations Protection Force, that managed the food for the UNPROFOR forces. I met some of the Canadian soldiers, and when I went up to the upper floors of the Holiday Inn, above my room, I would watch the shelling of the city from above, and I could actually gauge the gunfire by sound and then zero in on where the position was the fire was coming from and I was able to actually see activity of artillery and tanks being moved back and forth. I could follow tracers back and in the evenings I could see the muzzle flashes of guns and in the morning it was easy to identify where those guns were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were you able, from making those observations, to ascertain on whose territory those locations were, in other words, who controlled the territory where you spotted those sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was very easy to me and I pointed it out to Canadians and other journalists who were with me, CBS news and Italian news. There was a great news crew there. I was able to get a tank position and another firing position pointed out and they all filmed it and the next morning we saw where it was, above Grbavica, which was a Republik Srpska controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, in fact, whether you can name just some examples of these kind of positions and state at this stage, you know, roughly where they were, whether they were north, south, west, or east of the city. So I mean, can you give us some examples of places that you identified this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has the objection to the question put by my learned colleague. The question was to explain the positions, and the witness has not told us that he had any knowledge of what the positions were that we were talking about and at what time. This is a very general question indeed. We do not know what positions and whose positions you're referring to. I believe that my learned colleague should be a bit more specific when putting this question, and whose territory. I don't know what territory is meant here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, let me just try to see whether I can clarify the issue. I see as one of the answers, it's on my screen at 164258 that the witness is saying I was able to get a tank position and other firing position pointed out, and they all filmed it. So it was my understanding that the question was referring to the positions mentioned by the witness. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but what positions? We do not know what positions are meant. The witness simply said, "I saw positions." If my colleague could specify this question is bit further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, if you would agree to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I can save the Court time. I'll just rephrase it slightly. I don't agree with the objection, but I'm happy to save time and just rephrase, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have mentioned -- I've asked you whether you took any observations to try and ascertain some places where you thought you saw sources of fire of shelling or whatever on the city. Now, you have mentioned a couple of locations. You said something about a tank location and another firing point. Can you please tell the Court, Mr. Ashton, where exactly those locations you referred to are for the tank position and the other gun position and indicate where they are in relation to the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. Both positions were -- one position was above Grbavica, which I can't remember the side of the city that's on, but -- east, west, north, and south. I can't -- I'm out of track on which way the city is laid out now. I've forgotten that. But Grbavica, I could tell you clearly the areas. Trebevic, just below the mountain, below the ski lift, is where I saw one of the guns firing from and the other is obviously Grbavica, which I had later gone over to visit on several occasions and the gun was there when I was there. The tank was at the top of the hill there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And do you know what the name of that hill was, the other hill?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: There's a monument there at the top of the hill above Grbavica. It's Vrace, I think. I can't remember the name of the towns. I don't know the Serbian-Croat names any more because it's been a long time for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, we can get to discussing some of these locations more on a -- a little later on. Mr. Ashton, so you have made reference to shelling and sniping in the city at that time. Can you give just any indication of the amount of shelling and frequency and the amount of sniping and frequency that you observed in the July 1992? And I appreciate this is an early period, so we need to be brief on the point, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, I mean, July 1992, October, September, it didn't matter. It was fairly consistent all during that time except I was out for a little while. In July 1992 there was heavy shelling morning, noon, and in the early evenings. But that pattern continued on from throughout the war, as far as I could see. There was also a lot of sniping individually in the morning and then there was large amounts of sniping in different areas, but sometimes it would be very heavy. A few days it would be light. It was never -- there was never any consistency to it except for patterns of heavy shelling during a certain part of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when you had returned to Sarajevo, you've already made some reference to September, but when you returned to Sarajevo, how were things at that time? This is now into the month of September, late September.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of September, when I was first back from Germany and late August right into the early part of September, September and October were just -- they were disastrous for Sarajevo. I stayed in PTT for a while before I moved down town and the shelling throughout the city was so heavy that we were constantly on code red for Sarajevo. The UN forces were on code red. We were constantly warned about movement throughout the city by UNPROFOR command. We could stand in the window of the PTT, we could see the shells come down in the middle of a group of civilians who were walking down the boulevard, the main boulevard outside the window. It was very heavy constantly and there were several days when Republika Srpska command told UNPROFOR, told the people that I was with there and the UNPROFOR commander would notify us at UNHCR told us that we shouldn't go out because they said they were not going to stop shelling. They were trying to blow up the airport bridge, for example, one day in late September, to keep anyone from travelling across the bridge. In doing that, they were also trying to -- they hit the apartment complexes right in that area. It was very heavy throughout, all the way through the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That being said, do you recall -- were you, though, out and about in the city of Sarajevo during this period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I went out every day, no matter what. I travelled back and forth to the hospitals and I travelled up to visit people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, therefore, witness the actual impact of shells around the city of --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Indeed, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And at that time, in late September 1992 and moving on into the winter of 1992, can you give some indication to the Court of the kind of targets that appeared to be hit by those shells?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yeah. There were several incidents in which I was driving down the road. One evening in particular, there were camera crews from international and local television that were there with you me. An apartment complex was deliberately shelled and set on fire. I saw that on more than one occasions but I remember that specific incident because people were trying to climb out from the burning building and being shot at from across the Grbavica area. There was many incidents in which I was driving into an area and I would see an entire area of houses just sporadically shelled. I was in the Holiday Inn one day and I watched a tank come out on a hill in October I saw this earlier in July but I saw it again in October coming out and just fire into a neighbourhood of homes and I had just come from that area and there was no military activity up there that I could see. In fact, there were civilians out on the street. So it was a lot of sporadic, random shelling of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when you saw these particular places, like apartment blocks and houses receiving shell hits, were you able to observe whether there was any other form of military presence there, whether there were any vehicles, weapons, troops of any description?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No. I very rarely saw the Bosnian forces except walking to and from a position, but the thing is they were not -- most of them were not armed because at that point early in the war they didn't have any weapons except for the ones on the front lines which they traded. When the one came in unarmed, he would take the weapon from the other person who was on the line and they didn't -- you didn't see any military equipment like tanks because the Bosnians didn't have the heavy hardware that was on the other side of the front line, on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you at any time, however, see the effects of shells landing on other targets which might have been commercial or military or things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. There was an attack which lasted for an hour right next to the PTT building which hit a factory. The firemen came out to fight the fire and then of course there was a lull in the shelling and as soon as the firemen arrived they started firing again, the shells started coming in again. There were several -- the hospital was hit, the State Hospital was hit right in front of me one day when I was there. And I was at a funeral up in the cemetery, in the Lion's cemetery just below Kosevo hospital, and I was looking back over my shoulder while I was at this funeral and the shells hit in the hospital compound and before I could get out of the cemetery the shells started to fall in the cemetery, right around the area where the funeral was being held. In fact, all six or seven of the shells that came in landed right in the area of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you say when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That happened on two occasions. It was once in October that I remember very clearly and then again earlier in July, when I went to a funeral for a friend of mine that I had met there in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you are standing, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness has been recounting the events which happened prior to the period covered by the indictment for more than an hour, I would like to ask my learned colleague to reply as to why this is relevant. Why is it relevant for the witness to go on for about an hour talking about July and August, since this pertains to the period of time prior to the period of time covered by the indictment? And I would really like my colleague to explain why this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, would you respond to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. In the sort of general sense, I had actually concluded asking in the more general sense of his earlier experiences in Sarajevo and I propose going to certain specifics which albeit by way of date may predate the indictment. I think the relevance will become clear in terms of identification of specific locations. These will be locations which have relevance very much so to incidents, encounters and experiences that this witness will offer in relation to the years 1993 and half of 1994. But it sets the background as to the locations he identified and how he did so. So I would crave the Court's indulgence just to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Blaxill. The objection is rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like one more moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There's just one particular thing I would like to bring to your attention. You made reference to a gun position that you identified somewhere below mount Trebevic, and was there a particular incident in 1992 that enabled you to make that particular identification, perhaps in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, there just -- there are a lot of incidents in 1992, but I remember being in the hospital and at the Holiday Inn both when shelling occurred from that position at Trebevic, and I was able to see where the shells were coming from, especially in the evening when it got dark. There was still firing. There was one incident where a vehicle was hit in the street that was driving by the Holiday Inn on the main boulevard, in which a woman was either killed or seriously wounded but not got out but her driver did. There was a incident in front of the hospital which several people were wounded in July of that year. The shells came from the same position. You could see -- well, you could hear the shells coming down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there a particular area by the Holiday Inn where you identified from an impact that that was the site in Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to particularly think of one incident that comes to mind, but there are many in that period in July. I can't recall right now what it is that really sticks out in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You made some reference to the cable car, the street and in relation to the cable car and that there was a site in that location. Do you remember the name of that site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No. No, I can't recall it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Although you can't recall the name of the site, is that a place that you only identified from a distance or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, let me correct -- I don't -- let me correct myself. From the cable car, which the cable car on the mountain on Trebevic is what I've referred to as where one of the position is, and that's where, yeah, I definitely -- in fact, I went up to visit that position at a later time and I was told by the forces that were there that, you know, that's where they had one of the best vantage points for hitting downtown and the Presidency area and the area of Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when you said you later visited that place, was that after September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was in March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you visit it at any time after March 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a few visits up in the front lines areas of the Republika Srpska, and that was particularly one spot I stopped at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And there was -- was there a place adjacent to the Holiday Inn hotel where you made any identification relating to sniping rather than shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. There was an incident in which a woman got shot in front of me, which I tried to rescue, which was a horrific incident. She had tried to run across the street at the corner in front of the old Red Cross building, two blocks away from the Presidency, between the Presidency and the Holiday Inn hotel the main intersection there where the sniping was always very heavy. And a gentleman before her had been shot through the hand. I started to work on him because I crossed the street. There was a shot fired at me but they missed. I started working on the wounded gentleman and then there was another shot and she fell. She was shot through the leg. So I turned around and ran back out to get her, and I pulled her on to my legs because they opened fire several times must faster from the area of Trebevic. The bullets kept coming down and hitting the street around us. And as I pulled her on me, there was a loud shot and she got shot in the neck, in the throat, and at that point she was dead. There was no way I could save her. So I rescued myself and backed out from under her and got out of the line of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you make any observations that helped you ascertain where that fire may have come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, because they were using tracers. Every four or five shots was a tracer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was it that you observed that made you think you knew the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: You could see where the fire was coming from above the Jewish cemetery at the treeline there. But also the angle of the bullet would come down, and you could see it hit the street and then spark up at a low angle from the impact point, which indicated it was fired from a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when did this particular incident take place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I don't recall the date of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give me a season and a year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- that incident was in the early spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about close to the Holiday Inn itself? Did you have any particular -- make any particular observations of a location there in connection with the sniping?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Not directly, except there was gunfire coming across the river from Grbavica directly into the city, between the buildings, near the university and near the Holiday Inn and near the museum. But I found out later from the people that I'd met over in Grbavica that that's where they had their front line set up and that's where they were firing at people when they crossed the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you say they had their front line set up and they were firing. To whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: When I went over to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You're referring to the "Serb side"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The Republica Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: By that, do you mean the military of the--

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, the military. I was given a few tours over there, and they showed me where their lines were, and I went into some of the rooms where the windows were knocked out and sandbags were built up in the back of rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When did those incidents take place? We may refer back to them later, but when did that sort of thing take place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The first time I went down to Grbavica was probably June of 1993, and then of course I continued to go down there to the pharmacy and to the medical clinic to take medical supplies. And on several occasions, I was invited by the Serbs to sit down and have a drink with them, and they took me around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And again, those locations that you referred to, or the places you saw the impact of shots, did you see at those times any military presence there? I.e., were there any weapons or armoured vehicles or troops or anything when you saw those shots?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. By the way, can I refer back to a question you asked me just a little while ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Because there was one incident that came to mind, a shocking incident. I was at the Presidency with the rest of the press corps in Sarajevo, and a couple of us from the Detroit Free Press and CNN were walking back towards the Holiday Inn, and I heard the guns go -- the mortars go off at a position --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You heard the request. Would you please try to follow on the screen the questions, and once they have been written down, that you only start answering them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Okay. I will start that incident again. We were returning from the Presidency after a press conference, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can I ask you when this was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. This was in October of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I had just returned from Germany. I started up a side street between the State Hospital and the Presidency. I decided to take a small side street that I take to protect myself when there's heavy sniping, and there was sniping going on at that time. A shell had just landed five minutes prior to that while I was in the Presidency, and I came out and the shell landed next to a Mercedes Benz in front of the Presidency, spun the Mercedes Benz around, killed both the occupants of the car. I stopped to photograph that for a few seconds. Then as I proceeded on, my colleague from the Detroit Free Press was behind me and following me by about a minute, and I turned right to go up this little side street into a protected area, next to an old mosque that had already been destroyed by artillery. And just as I got to the corner where I would have gone into the little square there, I saw all the people in the square talking. There were some kids. There was a girl standing there with her dog and a few older people sitting on a bench in front of an apartment building there. I heard the thump of a mortar and then there was a loud crash, and that -- with that, the entire square was -- everyone in the square went down on the ground. And I was only protected because I hadn't stepped out into the area where the mortar fire -- the shrapnel hit the walls. And they fired two more rounds which landed in the area but did not land in that particular square, but one landed right beside the hospital, which was only about 40 metres away, and another one landed right behind one of the buildings where the square was. By then I had turned around and I could pinpoint on Trebevic that they were firing the mortar from that position. It was a silent, still day. I remember it very clearly. And I could hear the outgoing shell after the explosion, the thump of the outgoing mortar, at which point I started doing medical triage. I put my cameras down, and the photographer of the Detroit Free Press, he did take pictures of that, and there were other journalists who came along. The girl I started to treat had lost her leg and was wounded very badly in the arm. We were afraid we were going to have -- we took her to the hospital. Dr. Nakas, the surgeon, Abdulla Nakas, decided he was going to have to take off her arm. But the father, I found out, was one of the people that I went to try to help, and he was hit in the head with shrapnel and several small shrapnel wounds throughout his body. He died, and other victims in that square died as well. All together there were five shells that I remember, and then it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ashton, can you -- we've been talking about certain locations that you identified as Bosnian-Serb-held places with artillery or the like. Do you recall the name of Bistrik Kula as a location near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And where was Bistrik Kula?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Bistrik Kula is also in the area of Trebevic, by the cable lines, by the cable car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you have any particular reason to take notice of that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, because there was a gun position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And do you recall what sort of guns were fired from there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, there was an anti-aircraft gun or a -- there was also a 12-millimetre -- what they called a Daska [phoen], D-s-h-k-a, whatever, and I actually went up there later on and visited that area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you -- can you give us the dates between which you paid visits to that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That again was after June 1993. In March I began going to Pale to take medicines to the hospital, the Serb hospital in Pale, and travelling around to Grbavica and to other areas in the Serb-controlled territory to check on their medical needs. And I eventually started getting stopped at checkpoints, and when Serb soldiers knew I had medicines, they asked me for help for their families. And as I got to know them, they asked me to stop and have coffee with them or have a drink of slivovitz with them, and eventually they started inviting me to come and sit down with them, and that's how I was able to go to these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you just -- we will get into that in some detail a little later, but at this stage, Mr. Ashton, can you indicate how many such positions you must have -- you did visit during the course of the year 1993 and the first part of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: At least -- at least ten positions. There were other areas that I didn't see as significant, but as far as gun positions, there were at least ten, but about six of them I'm really -- I was really familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, I just noticed something. You made a reference, when you described that last incident, referring to the date October 1993, and you then made reference to shortly after returning from Germany. Would you -- are you correct in the dates you gave at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: For which incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When did you come back from Germany? I think you made reference to the lady and the dog.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I got back during the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you made a reference to this incident being in October, after your return from Germany, so would that be 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please: During the winter of 1992 to 1993, prior to your starting your medical aid, NGO, what was the shelling and sniping like in the city of Sarajevo during those winter months?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: 1992 and 1993 was very heavy, concentrated periods of shelling and sniper fire. There would be a few days where it was quiet, but for the majority of the time it was consistent. I mean, you never knew when. There was no indication. There were times, like I said earlier, of the day when it could be very heavy. 7.00 in the morning through about 9.00 in the morning it would be very heavy. Then you'd see or hear heavy shelling around 1.00 in the afternoon, maybe early in the evening. But there were times when it would shell all day long, they would snipe all day long. But later on, in the end of 1993, more towards 1994, there were several agreements to have ceasefires, so there were periods of a week or two weeks at a time in 1994 where it got very quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And again, during that shelling, during that period, what impression did you get in terms of what was being targeted, or rather, what was being hit by the shells and by the snipers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The majority of things -- the targets I saw were civilian targets. I saw a lot of people go out to water lines. These were targeted specifically. And I saw people trying to cut down trees. I saw snipers actually shoot at people. We had a group of people right outside the PTT who attempted to cut down trees in late October or December when it got cold, and in January again they would come back for what was left of the trees as they were slowly being cut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you said a group of people right outside the PTT. What sort of people are you talking about? Would they be civilians, male, female?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The majority of them were old people. I mean, you saw a lot of geriatrics, women bent over, men with an axe, and there were quite a few children. Most of the children would go out and do the cutting for some of their families, I assume. In one particular incident we had a shelling right outside the PTT in which three people were killed, two others were wounded carrying wood that they had just cut, which -- several people from UNHCR office and the UNPROFOR team witnessed. The French did finally go out and assist them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, sir, did you ever see any soldiers mixed with those people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No. There were no soldiers in that shelling. I very --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry. I was going to say or people wearing military clothing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Or appearing so?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No. There were no soldiers there. And the other fact of that particular incident was the UNPROFOR commander there in Sarajevo would have called up the Serb liaison. At that time it was Major Brane, and he told him to stop the shelling. He ordered him to stop the shelling. So Brane told him he would see what he could do about it and then the shelling continued throughout the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you again give us the date or as close to the date that this happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That particular incident was also in December of 1993. I can't give you the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I had previously asked you, in fact we were talking about the winter of 1992 to 1993, so you've just given a December. Are you sure you mean 1993 or do you mean --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was December 1992. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was the wood cutting exercise you referred to the one that took place by daylight or at some other time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It was a cloudy day. It was misty and very cold. It was close to -- it was about at least an hour before dark, but it was clear. I mean, you could see the hills and you could see into the city, all over. I could see all the way to the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did people ever try to go out at night to gather -- to chop trees and gather wood?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Frequently, and when -- occasionally a women would be brought in shot at the hospital or someone would be brought in shot in the evening cutting wood. I would ask how this could happen if they were in the dark and I was told that the Serb soldiers had night vision equipment and they could see when people were in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you personally observe the night-time cutting of wood by people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Along the main boulevard downtown all the way out to the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Again, if you observed these people doing it, can you say whom they were, civilian, military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the old people tried to go out more at night to do the wood cutting because it was safer for them. They couldn't move as fast and they knew it was risky to travel during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you personally observe casualties sustained by people at night who were cutting wood?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion I stopped and helped someone into the vehicle who had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you have made those observations of this nocturnal activity did you at any time see the presence of soldiers or weapons or military vehicles which would attract or could legitimately attract fire to that place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No. There was generally a curfew in Sarajevo. The police had a curfew and the only activity, the people who could move would be the police or the military and generally the military had a standard rotation at certain hours of the day. Their forces were so thin that they were terribly, terribly stretched out along the front lines so you didn't see much of them in the city. They were pretty much strapped to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just excuse me a second, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And during -- we've been talking about the night-time wood chopping. Now, when you stopped with your Land Rover to help somebody, when did that take place? In what year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was January of 1993, that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I took the victim to the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ashton, in fact, I would like to move to, briefly to the State Hospital. Where was it that you were staying in Sarajevo when you had returned from Germany after your treatment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: When I returned I went straight down to the State Hospital to let the doctors know that the German doctors wanted to send medicine, and I met both Abdulah and Bakir Nakas again with whom I had built a relationship when I was there the first time, and they invited me to stay at the hospital. If I wanted a room, I need a room, I could stay there. I had an option to stay at the PTT, but I went ahead and chose to stay at the hospital because I thought it would be easier for me to go from there to Kosevo hospital to do an analysis of both hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So staying in the hospital, what was the situation regarding the shelling and sniping in terms of any effect on the State Hospital while you were resident there at the end of 1992 and into the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The State Hospital was significantly damaged in late 1992 and on into 1993. Every day a shell would be fired into the hospital. Whether it was a heavy shell or anti-aircraft shell, there would be always something hitting that hospital. On certain times you were not sure if it was deliberately targeted and it was just a straight bullet that hit it. But oddly enough, every morning around 7.00 a.m., we would get hit with an anti-aircraft shell low in the hospital, come off of Trebevic and slam into the building. It happened around noon every day, but there were incidents in which the shells came directly into the hospital facade. It was obvious when targets were hit directly and continued on for five minutes that that was the particular target and I saw that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you say -- you say you saw that on several occasions. Can you give us a time span as to when you actually witnessed that? Again, was any of this after September 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: One particular incident I remember on September 23rd when the hospital took three major hits from two sides, one from the front and two shells hit it from the east, from towards Pale. But that day was a very crucial day because we had so many wounded people from the street come in and a shell landed just as some of the wounded were arriving and wounded more that had gone out to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've referred to the east side, you've referred to the front of the hospital. Do you know the area, or areas that the front of the hospital faced?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The front of the hospital faced directly across to Grbavica, directly into the Jewish cemetery area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've made reference -- I will ask you that. Can you indicate to us which forces had control of the Jewish cemetery area and had control of Grbavica area at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Below the Jewish cemetery was in control of Bosnian forces. Above the cemetery and where the shelling for that particular day that the hospital was being fired at, was just above -- there was a tree line there and there was a tank or a big gun in there firing into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You personally witnessed this with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you state to us about how far away from the hospital we have, let us say, where you said the Bosnian-held area, the bottom of the cemetery, how far was that from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The Bosnian-controlled territory in front of the hospital made an angle and up the hill. To the right of the hospital the Bosnian-controlled territory ran right along the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How far was that from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Maybe a hundred metres, 110 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how far -- how much further was it from the hospital to the front line of the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: About 450, 500 metres, 400 metres. I'd say 400 metres easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And behind that point some 400 metres away , was all the territory behind that under the control of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you have witnessed those shellings. Was there another incident shortly after in September that was significant, I mean September 1992 at that point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Well, the incident, like I said, the September 23rd, was one of the most serious I saw at that time, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may interfere, I see that for the record, you went too fast again. Could you please, Mr. Blaxill, resume your questioning at 17.24.33 so that we can hear the answer and then continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. At that point I asked you, Mr. Ashton: Behind the point, some 400 metres from the hospital, where there were the first SRK troops, was all the territory behind that under the control of the SRK? I think you replied Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are where we left off, then. And I then asked you: You witnessed those shellings, was there another incident in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So I think everything is on the record now, Your Honours. I'm just sorry that the pair of us went a little quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To go back to that, I'm just tracking your answer. My apologies. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes. You were just staying that September 23rd was one of the most serious incidents you saw at that time because --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: We had more than 40 casualties come in immediately to State Hospital. Others were taken to Kosevo hospital. One particular couple I remember, Sandra and her boyfriend both had been wounded, Svetozar. She had a very serious leg injury and I started working on her. I cut off the pants leg and her boyfriend had also a serious leg injury, and I thought both of them were going to have their legs amputated. There was a woman who told me she -- I went over to another woman who told me she was just waiting for a bus because the Sarajevo -- the government there in Sarajevo had decided to try to start running the buses just to try to give people some sense of normalcy in the city. And there were several people waiting at that stop and that's where most of the victims had come from. In the case of Sandra, she later told me that she and her boyfriend had stopped to help a wounded woman and when they went out, they knew the risk that there would be -- after the first two shells there would be a pause and then there would be more shells coming to wound the rescuers. But she said they couldn't leave that woman there, but the woman turned out to be expired. So when they were dealing with her injury, the third, fourth and fifth shell came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Again, did you, whilst you were in the State Hospital, do anything to try and identify the sources of fire for the shells you saw coming?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Earlier -- when that attack began, I was up on the fourth floor. In fact, I had just gotten out of bed. And that's how I was able to gauge the first shells that were coming in, I could tell were artillery. They were not mortar, they were artillery rounds and they were coming from the direction of Pale. I was able to do what I usually did when I heard artillery fire, I would count the seconds, and it took about 13 seconds, almost exactly 13 seconds from the time of the shell fire to the time of impact was about a 9-second whistle before the shell impacted, and I was able to determine where those positions were generally but not until 1993 was I actually able to go and see that gun position on the Republika Srpska side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, if there would be a point nearby where it would be suitable to have a break. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions probably would reach such a point, Your Honour. I will do so expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, so you have just described you did this, and were you therefore able to say or are you able to say where that particular place was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the name of the place. It's not on my mind. I can show you on a map. It's very easy to get to by road from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And that being said, was that a place you subsequently visited, I believe you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you -- and when did you visit and how many times?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: 1993, but 1994 is when I remember going there and actually -- it was actually very difficult to get there. I was told not to stop on that side by the Serb military, but one day I was travelling through and I stopped in the town, in the little village there and ended up meeting some people and the soldiers took me over to where the guns were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, at this point, I think, Mr. President, we could conveniently break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. We will then adjourn until 10 minutes to 6.00, almost 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll just wait until the witness has been brought in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said we're just waiting until the witness has been brought in the courtroom and then you may proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I should like to inform the Chamber that I have just received two statements from my colleagues, the statements that were taken by them in 1996 and 1998 respectively, concerning two witnesses, the statements by two witnesses that are going to be examined. I have just received the statements, and I should just kindly ask my colleagues to be more efficient in that respect, because we are in an unfair situation like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, they are in fact translations that have just been received from the Translation Service into the language of the accused and of course having just received those translations, we have immediately passed them on. The original statements in one of the official languages, namely English in this case obviously have been part of prior disclosure. So it is only a question of the translations that have now been supplied to my learned friends today as they've come into our hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much for giving us the floor. There has been a delay in respect of certain exhibits. These statements were taken three or more years ago, and I believe that this period of time should be sufficient for the purposes of translation. The Defence wishes to state that it is impossible for them to prepare themselves, because these exhibits, these statements, could not have been given to the accused. But I think that by presenting them now at the trial, this is not something that is compatible with the rules that we are all required to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We all know that this Tribunal has great problems as far as the Translation Services are concerned, so I'm afraid I can't change that overnight. On the other hand, I'd like to be sure that this will not be more prejudicial to the rights of the accused as it is as such, because is there any -- do you have any idea, Mr. Blaxill, when these witnesses will be called of which the statements have been given in translation to the Defence only recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The translation that has been given in respect of one witness is in fact in respect of a supplemental information sheet, and that document relates to a witness who will be testifying two down the line from Mr. Ashton. So we have Mr. Ashton, we have a further witness, and then the relevant witness for that supplemental information sheet. The other witness referred to is a lady whose statement was served a long time ago in the English version, and that witness we would not imagine being called at least for the best part of another week. And it is a fairly short statement. So in that sense, the translation -- there's plenty of time, I would respectfully suggest, for the accused to read the statement in his own language. As I say, it's been served in an official language long since. The other document that has been supplied, again in a translation form, is for a gentleman who is a psychiatrist who is on the list and would not be called for at least two or more weeks. And the final document is translation of a few brief annotations on a map which is a disclosed exhibit in respect of Mr. Ashton, and that's been translated into B/C/S even though those brief annotations will in due course be read, at least I will be inviting Mr. Ashton at the appropriate time to read those annotations into the record and they will be in all the languages we could require. So that is the position regarding those documents, Your Honours. As I say, we have done what we have done as promptly as possible upon receipt from the Translation Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, do I understand the matter correctly if I tell you that we have received tonight, at 1800, documents that the accused was not able to see or examine, and we know that he could not have discussed the statements with their lawyers. In respect of the examination of the witness which is supposed to be held tomorrow. And once again, we are talking about the documents which have been in the possession of the OTP since 1996. Or have I misunderstood the matter? Please note that I am prepared to spend my first night in prison tonight, but I would need a specific authorisation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, would you please respond to this objection which has been repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The map in question, this is the document my learned friend I think is referring to vis-a-vis the witness for tomorrow, namely, Mr. Ashton. That document was effectively marked up at the time he completed his statement with our office on the 14th of November this year, and -- I'm so sorry. November 2001. And it was immediately after the conclusion of that statement on the 14th of November, 2001 that it was then submitted for translation purposes. So that the statements were duly translated and all relevant documentation. And these annotations, as I say, are very brief, and they have -- as I say, this is a document I would be having Mr. Ashton read into the record of the Court anyway and you will have a perfect translation of all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I first ask you a question. Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I answer your question in French, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the question remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My answer is I can understand -- I read English perfectly, but the accused does not understand English, nor does he understand French. I'm talking about the rights of the accused, not about the rights of the Defence. The accused doesn't speak any of the official languages of the Tribunal, and the right of the accused should be safeguarded in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I just put a question to you whether you could read English, and the reason why I put this question to you is that I wanted to know in what respect you could be of supplementary service to guarantee the rights of the accused. Because I think it's part of the work of Defence counsel to do whatever he can in order to inform his client about things that are happening during the proceedings even if they are not -- if they're not perfect at the moment. Just -- I just wanted to know whether you are totally blocked, if the Defence as a whole team would be totally blocked by just receiving an English copy or that only two members of the Defence team, if I could say that the Defence team consists of the accused and two counsel, whether only part of the Defence team was blocked. Because from my considerations that may have some importance. Then as far as short annotations on maps are concerned, the Chamber would like to give the Prosecution the opportunity to proceed, but whenever it comes to a point where you say, "We have to discuss this with our client," even if it was briefly, then you'll be given an opportunity for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thank the Chamber for this opinion, but what I wanted to say and what I need to reiterate here is the following: It is possible that these documents which I have had in English since very recently, that they contain things which could be brought up by the accused, who has detailed and specific knowledge about the events, the knowledge which is lacking on the part of the counsel, and that is precisely the reason why we have the Rules that we have, that we have to follow. I don't know always what kind of questions I need to ask. It is not that I want to impose any cultural obstacles to the work of the Tribunal. I am talking about the necessity, the need that we all have and that the accused has. The accused has to be given opportunity to prepare himself for his defence. Although my mission is to help him, and this is something that we all have to do here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and I'm addressing both the Defence and the Prosecution, of course the Chamber is quite unhappy with this -- with this late translation to be provided to the accused, and I may underline again that of course this is not what it should be. And it speaks for itself that if the Defence would have at a later stage, after the accused has been able to read these documents, would come back to the issues, I think we'll have to give them the opportunity. And I do understand that it's always a second choice, because the first choice would be to be properly prepared for cross-examination of the witness. But let's try to do our best and also may I ask the accused to read these translations as soon as possible. So at the earliest date possible you can come back to it when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. We should like to propose that during the cross-examination, contrary to the common usage, this cross-examination be conducted by both Defence counsel, because we have this linguistical problem which is not our fault, and I hope that the Chamber will give us permission to proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber gives you permission to proceed in that manner. Then, Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed now in the examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, we have been describing certain observations that you had made from the State Hospital in the wintertime of 1992 and into early 1993. You had made reference to some shelling from the east side, from the direction of Pale. Did you, from that hospital, make any observations that identified any other sources of fire which resulted in hits upon the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The particular incident on the 23rd of September, 1992 was from heavy artillery coming from the east of the city, in the morning, that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what about any hits on the front side of the building that faced directly to Grbavica? Did you ever make any observations by night or by day that indicated the source of fire of those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: During -- yes, I did. I did make identification of shells that were fired from that side of the hospital, facing Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you tell us when the first time was you made such an observation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The first time was back in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you make any other such observations -- after July of which year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you make any subsequent observations later that year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. September of 1992, October of 1992, December of 1992, January of 1993. It was a continuous event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what were the observations that you made on those occasions that gave you an indication of the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: At two points in specific, I could see the artillery piece being moved into place, into position. Keep in mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, on which dates or as precisely as you can remember on what dates you saw those pieces of artillery and where they were being manoeuvred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Because of the time lapse the dates are very difficult for me to remember exactly. I do remember in October one incident from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And are we talking --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: On the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is that October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You referred to a tank. What did you observe on that occasion, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: On that occasion there was a tank at the top of -- above Grbavica on the hill on the road to Pale, right on the edge of the road, which fired into the hospital. I went up to one of the upper floors after the shell hit to take photographs, to take pictures, and when I was sitting there I could hear the second shot fire. I didn't see the tank at that point but it was in the direction of Grbavica. And then the third shot that fired I actually saw where the tank was located. The tank withdrew after the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In which direction did the tank withdraw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It backed up behind some trees and rocks up at the top of the hill there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And where was that place in relation to the lines, the confrontation lines in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Again, that was up on the road to Pale, up above Grbavica, beyond Grbavica, well into Republika Srpska territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you observe such an action again in respect of that tank at any other time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I had seen that tank earlier in July. It fired into a group of houses next to the Jewish cemetery. That tank came out and that was one of the incidents I pointed out to CBS news and they had a cameraman film it while I was talking photographs. One thing I wanted to say here was I had a camera with a 300 millimetre lens, a Nikon camera with a 300 millimetre extra definition lens, ED lens, so I had very good vision, and I also had a 1,000 millimetre lens so I could bring things in very close. Once I could identify where fire was coming from, I could clearly see where the position of a tank or artillery or machine-gun was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Aside from the location of that tank, was there anything else about it that indicated whose tank it was?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down a bit for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Just the location of the tank was all I could really tell at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you said you had made the sighting in October 1992, then the earlier sighting in July. Did you see a tank or that tank again after that date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It would be very difficult for me to say that I saw that particular tank; however, the position was exactly the same position as before, or the July incident was the same position as the October incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there an incident again after October?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, there was an incident after October, in February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And on that occasion, what was it you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The tank appeared again when I was at the hospital and fired down into the area of the Holiday Inn near the museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see anything of a military nature down there, troops, guns, vehicles, in the place that got hit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any military activity. However, there were civilians on the street crossing -- at that time there were metal barriers and there were also UNPROFOR troops Ukranian and French soldiers stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see any of the defensive troops of Sarajevo, the ABiH there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Negative. I saw no defensive troops there. I did at that point see the civilian scatter and run for cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How many shells were fired on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Three that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Three on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: At that point I left the area too, because I was in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And after the three shells were fired, did you observe what happened with the tank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. No. I didn't observe what happened with the tank on that particular incident, because, like I said, I was -- occasionally when I was in the hospital area like that, I would take a picture and I would get out of the window, because usually if I stayed in the window too long I could draw sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you -- you said you could draw sniper fire. Did it happen on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Not on that occasion, but on previous occasions it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you indicate to us any previous occasions and locations where you have drawn sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I drew sniper fire from the windows of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How many shots do you recall being fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Two shots were fired. One shot actually injured an Italian cameraman who was with me, the casing of the bullet when it broke up against the window frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And whereabouts were you when you were fired upon from the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I was in a room. It was the same evening the tank had been firing at the houses across from Grbavica down into the houses, just below Bistrik, near the Jewish cemetery area. And we waited after we watched one of the houses catch fire. As darkness came the tank fired a few more rounds into that housing area, particularly in that area of that house. Then I backed out of the room in the hallway of the Holiday Inn and the Italian camera crew came and I explained to them what was going on. So they came out into the room, and I specifically warned one of the gentleman to put out his cigarette, which he did not do, and that's what I assume drew the sniper fire into that window. The first shot came in, he turned around to get out and a second shot hit the window frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of the time of evening that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was shortly after dark. It was dark outside. Probably around 8.00, 8.30 that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps you could remind us of the date of that event, when it occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That particular event was in July. It was before I was wounded, but not the exact date I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us any of your experiences of drawing sniper fire later on in that year after September 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. In the window of the hospital I was taking pictures one day and I thought that I was fairly safe because I stayed back in a room, but I was in a room where the front had been knocked out by artillery shell. So enough light apparently was getting in that somebody could watch me move around the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. And can you state whereabouts in the hospital, you mean State Hospital, I presume?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: State Hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you say whereabouts in the State Hospital that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: On the fifth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what side of the building, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Facing Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you again give us an indication of the date when this happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That happened in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was that the early or later part of September, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was the early part of September. It happened again in that same -- not in that particular room but in that hospital in October and again later on, when I was up higher in the hospital on another floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dealing with that first event, the event we're now describing from September 1992, what in fact happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: After the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you drew the fire, how many shots were fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Only one shot came in. It came very close to me and I backed out of the room as quick as I could get out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please keep in mind that slowing down now and then it is far better for the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to pace the conversation for the interpreters

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill if you would also read the transcript so that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm endeavoring to, Your Honour, but we do lapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's difficult I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's a problem when you both work in the same language. We do our best. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, can you give us an indication when the next event was that you drew fire of this type?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Something has just come to mind and I need to make a correction in earlier testimony. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If you have something you wish to correct, sir, yes, please tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The incident -- I just started thinking about the sniper fire and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mind the speeds.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I remembered that the incident which happened with the woman with the dog who lost the arm in the -- was wounded in the leg or lost her leg and the father who was killed was in July and not in October as I previously stated, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In July of which year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was July, because -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Now, what made me think about that was another incident which was right behind the Holiday Inn, close to that same area, which was a sniper incident in which I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That took place in September, early September of 1992. There was a Canadian contingent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again have to repeat. You really have to read until the question, Mr. Ashton, as far as you are concerned, is written on the screen. And Mr. Blaxill, until the response. I know, talking the same language makes it difficult, but you have to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, perhaps we could move on. You have made reference here to September of 1992, but early. Now, how early in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I guess it was around the 15th, mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. If you could tell us what happened on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I came out of the Holiday Inn to do my daily run down to the Presidency. It was early in the morning, about 8.00. And I had to run out the front door because there was a sniper who sporadically shot from one of three apartment buildings in Grbavica a journalist or anyone entering or leaving the front door of the Holiday Inn. And when I came out the door, I ran along the columns in the front, at which point I heard a loud pop of the larger-calibre gun that fired in the kitty-corner street behind the Holiday Inn, which was fired on every day and where people had been wounded and killed by the sniper. I saw an old woman and a young woman. It turned out to be her daughter, trying to cross the street, and the old woman froze in the middle of the street. A second shot was fired. It was a large-calibre round and it made a huge blue spark off the street. I laid my cameras down and her daughter was screaming for her to run, and I ran out and grabbed her and pulled her out of the street, and a third shot was fired at both of us, missing us by about a metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You referred to a third shot. Was that again a large-calibre round?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Large-calibre round. I told the Canadian UNPROFOR unit in the Holiday Inn immediately afterwards what happened. They brought an APC, an armoured personnel carrier, from the airport out and put it in that street. I went back out in the afternoon because the shooting had stopped, and I leaned against the armoured personnel carrier with my left arm and looked out to talk to one of the men in the armoured personnel carrier, and a shot hit the front of the armoured personnel carrier. The Canadian soldier in the carrier turned towards Trebevic as I ran away from the carrier, and another shot was fired, and they turned the personnel carrier towards Trebevic, in that direction on the street, towards Bistrik Kula, and continued to make observations, and then another shot was fired near the APC. And I found out later that the Canadians did identify the target area but did not fire back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. You referred to the APC. What colour was that APC?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: White with UN markings on the side, about a metre tall, and white -- on the front were the UN markings, on the front as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were the soldiers in the vehicle wearing any noticeable headgear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: They were wearing blue helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned saying the elderly lady and her daughter crossing the street. Can you say more precisely where that was? Do you remember the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: If I refer to a map, I can remember the name, and of course the street names have changed since I was there. There was a park between -- it was directly between Sarajevo State Hospital and Holiday Inn and it's a short little angle street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you've made reference to the sniping from a location in Grbavica. Can you please tell us on what basis you have ascertained which apartment block, where it was in relation to confrontation lines in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The Canadians again brought in an anti-sniper team. When a shot was fired from that building at a non-armoured white UN pick-up truck driven by two Canadian soldiers who had come to pick up food. Again, the APC was brought down from the airport. Soldiers disembarked and went into the Holiday Inn, to a higher floor. They waited for several hours and the sniper fired again. That evening, the sniper fired once more at a journalist coming in the front door, Kurt Short, from BBC, and the Canadians fired one shot back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Ashton, when was this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: This again was in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you indicate what part of September?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The end of September. It was almost the last -- it was right -- the day before my birthday, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
