utterances.text: Can you give us any other example of a sniping incident you had witnessed, let us say, during the winter and up to the spring of 1993, before you started your NGO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I had seen, again, people trying to cross the bridges, cross the river in central Sarajevo, especially in Novo Sarajevo. I would watch them stop and hide behind a tree or behind a wall and then jump up and run, and then the shot would be fired. I watched at a major intersection near the Energoinvest building, which was another one of the most dangerous intersections in all of Sarajevo, because the sniping was consistent at that intersection. It was a wide, broad area that looked up towards the corner of Hrasno district and Grbavica where they intersected, but there was clearly a sniping position that fired down into that every day, and I saw on --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Slow down a little, if you please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: -- on more than one occasion women and children shot at at that intersection, and one man that I remember very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you give us any dates or approximate dates when you witnessed --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: January in particular was bad at that intersection. Several times when I came to that intersection there were containers put up there, and I had to run too, because the shots were fired at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what kind of shots were they in terms that you were able to ascertain as to the calibre of weapon? Would these be small or larger?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It was equivalent to a 12-millimetre, 12.7, 50-calibre round.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And on those occasions, what sort of, let us say, frequency or not of the shots were there? Was this automatic fire, single-shot fire? What sort of things?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The sniping fire was almost on a regular basis a single-shot fire. It was clear that somebody was taking aim and taking care to fire and hit the target they were intending to hit. It was very rare that you would go into an intersection and draw rapid machine-gun fire. It happened on occasion, especially in vehicles. Sometimes when we were driving down Polje Pase [phoen], the main street that came towards the Presidency from the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Again, can you give me some dates or indicated dates when you encountered such automatic fire at that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: One particular incident I remember is in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: 1992, another incident in December that my vehicle was shot at. I was in a UNHCR vehicle, cleared marked. Again, it was shot at in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how many shots? Do you say that was automatic or single-shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: When I came down in October, there were several shots fired at my vehicle. I did not count the number. I saw two of them strike the street and I heard one hit a wall beside me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when you had those encounters with sniping, were there any other people around at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Just one or two people who -- at that time it was -- the day that I got shot at in October with the -- there was already sniping going on in the street all day long, so there were not many people out. When sniping was consistent on any given day, the people disappeared from the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: A little while back you made reference to the sniping on a number of women and "a man." Can you tell us something about the man in question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. The man was -- I remember him very well, and the reason I brought him up is because he was dishevelled. He was a middle-aged man. He was not young, he was not old, but he was -- I particularly noted that he seemed disoriented, and after he was shot at, he was shaking and talking to himself. I went across the intersection. I was shot at. And I stopped to ask him if he was okay, and he started to cry and begged me, "Why are they doing this? What have I done to them?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When that occurred, were you able to ascertain the source of the fire on that occasion? I hope I'm not repeating myself with the question. If you would, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I couldn't ascertain the direct source of the fire. I would assume it was from the angle -- if you were to walk -- on days when it was quiet, I was able to get on the other side of the metal barriers. These are cargo containers. It was of particular interest to me, because one of the US -- the US ambassador there at the time, Jakovic, had someone there who pointed out to me the way to find out where the fire is coming from is to get in the container or behind the container and look at the angle from where the bullet comes in and I was able to see that all the bullets marks were coming down from a high position. He actually had a man go into the container from the Presidency, from the US embassy and string draw where the bullets were coming from and they could tell exactly where they were coming from on the area of Bistrik Kula, above --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashton. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, you've made -- I know we've referred to this incident earlier in more connection with the ladies. Can you tell us, please, where, on what intersection, that incident you've just described took place involving the man?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Again, I need to look at the map to name the street. It's the -- the back route we took from the Holiday Inn or downtown to the PTT. The front route was much too dangerous. It was wide open to sniper fire, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It was right next to Energoinvest building. That's one marker I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you say if one was standing on the street facing either direction, where would you be facing towards, from Energoinvest if you looked down towards the source of fire? Where would you be looking at?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Above Hrasnica. The hill above Hrasnica, Trg Heroja, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And those locations you've just mentioned, in which territory were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: There's a big sports stadium on the Republika Srpska side, right at the front line. That's the area that the fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say the sports -- the area, was that area beyond that sports stadium, if you say that was the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Beyond that sports stadium, yes, or beside the sports stadium there were houses on a steep hill which --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you give an idea of how elevated a position that is? Is it very high, medium?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It's a very good height to fire down into that intersection. It's clearly visible from the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you've mentioned the way that the Americans arranged to have this testing done of the angle of fire inside the container using string. Can you say when and where that was done?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was done in early 1993, after the Holiday Inn had been fired on. Jakovic and the embassy staff when they first opened the new US embassy in Sarajevo, they worked out of the Holiday Inn, and one day shells were fired in the proximity of the rooms where the Americans were located, and there was heavy sniper fire. And Jakovic and his assistant Jennifer both began talking to me about someone who was working on their staff. I don't know if he was military or what his position was, but he was going to start doing examination. He just arrived in Sarajevo to assist with the identification of the weapons being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, do you recall whether this examination using the string technique was performed on the containers at the location where you said the incident happened with this man?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. They were performed at that location in front of the Presidency, and in three positions in front -- between the museum and the university and the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were they all done at about the same time, within --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: At that particular time they did all the measurements, but I also know that they all -- they continued to do it later on. They coordinated with the French G-4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And again, can you just remind us, please, of the date when the incident occurred with the man?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was either in December or January. It was really cold and it was -- it was a very cold day, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are we talking 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: 1992, 1993, right in that -- it was right around the holiday season there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To take you back for a moment to another set of incidents that you say you witnessed, and that's in relation to the bridges. Can you say how many of the bridges over the river were usable or were being crossed by people at the end -- towards the end of 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: At least five bridges that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were those bridges in any particular end of the town or were they --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Three of them were in the old town section and two of them were up in Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: About how far is it from the old town area to Novo Sarajevo in terms of those bridges?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Almost 1.500 metres, 2.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And was there any way that you could ascertain the source of fire down onto those bridges, where it came from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: For me, now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How close were the bridges to the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Three of them were probably about 800 metres in the old town section. The one near Trg Heroja was probably 500 metres from the corner of Grbavica and Trg Heroja front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon me, Mr. Ashton. I do apologise for the state of my voice. When you were in the State Hospital as a resident - and I'll just try and finish with this period of your time in Sarajevo - I believe you said you used to assess needs and things for your proposed supply of proprietary medicines in the future. Did you have much contact with patients within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And the staff?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Every day I would visit the hospital and meet with Dr. Nakas, Abdulah Nakas, occasionally with the hospital's director, Bakir Nakas, but especially the general doctors working in the emergency area, and I would do rounds with the doctors to see what the most critical needs were, almost on a daily basis, which gave me an opportunity to speak with patients about their injuries, about their needs. And it was normal in conversation to ask, "Where were you wounded? How were you wounded? Do you remember coming, being brought in?" And I was able to ascertain a lot of information from the parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give some idea -- I mean, having had that amount of contact with the patients, can you give us any idea of the -- during that period, the winter of 1992 into 1993, whether there were military patients there, you know, former soldiers, or civilians, and if so, in what ratio? And what about sort of the quantities of women or children or very old people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I did an assessment, which I gave to the World Health Organisation, over a one-month period, 30-day period, and discovered that the majority of the patients, and it turned out to be 80 per cent plus or minus 5 per cent, were civilian casualties who were not armed. There were very few males in that population. It was largely women and children. Of that percentage it was about 70 per cent women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did that, during your period of acquaintance --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did that sort of ratio change significantly, as far as you are aware, in your ongoing contact with the hospital and its staff and patients?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No. There was never a significant change. I asked one day about military casualties to one of the doctors, and he said because the forces were spread out, that they had a few clinics which they dealt directly with trauma injuries, on the front line, and there were not that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you inform us, please, when you actually performed that particular assessment that you did for the WHO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I'll try to think of the timing of that. It had to be close to the very last part of December of 1992, because Margaret was still there from Sweden and she was the WHO representative. She concurred that my figures were correct. She said it was a very high number, because she had gone on two occasions and found the same results.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you performed this assessment, did you do so over a given period, or was it on a --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. It was Over 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Over a 30-day period. Can you recall which 30-day period that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It was during the month of December, and it may have been early January when I finally concluded, of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, having described the damage to the State Hospital, did you have cause to visit any other hospitals within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the Kosevo Hospital centre at least twice a week, talked to doctors specifically about proprietary needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Over what period would you make those regular visits?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: That was throughout the entire time I was there, from 1992 to end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I may perhaps just interject that one question. When did you eventually then leave Sarajevo, Mr. Ashton?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: In the very end of 1995, of October 1995. I also visited the hospital in Dobrinja, which was hardly a hospital. It was a converted building into a hospital, out of necessity, that they couldn't transport people out of Dobrinja in the first period of the war, the first quarter of the war. In fact, it wasn't until 1993 that the road from Dobrinja was actually safe enough to transport people out. It was around April of 1993 the hospital -- casualties began coming into the city hospitals. And I also visited the tuberculosis hospital in Republika Srpska, near Lukavica, and also I worked with the hospital in Blazuj, the Serb hospital in Blazuj, and the Serb hospital in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you: Did you perform any kind of equivalent assessment type of work in any of the other hospitals as compared to the one you did at State?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: No, I didn't in the other hospitals, although on the Serb side I did determine that much of the problem was from disease and other illnesses, problems that they had, but there were very, very few casualties in the Serb hospitals. I did run into a few soldiers who were wounded on the front line in Pale hospital, where they were brought after treatment, closer to the front lines, because the distance was so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, then, in fact, just one final point regarding the assessment you did perform, and that is: Can you indicate the number of casualties who informed your, you know, your statistical base, if you like, for that assessment? Can you recall the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me -- I'm not quite sure I understand the question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I probably asked it rather clumsily, Mr. Ashton. How many casualties formed your survey? Was it 10, 100, 200? When you did the assessment --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: There were over 400 patients. Around 400 exactly almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. So you have made reference to other hospitals that you have visited, and I'd like to pursue just briefly at this stage the question of the Serb hospitals, Pale and I think it's Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Blazuj. Thank you. And can you give now from recollection any idea of again the percentage of people who would have been patients with just normal diseases or whatever and persons who were there through some kinds of injuries from violence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. The two doctors -- the three doctors, rather, running the three hospitals that I visited in Serb territory were very, very cooperative in allowing me access to patients and their figures. Their casualty figures were about 4 or 5 per cent from the war itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Five per cent -- four or five per cent of what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Their patients, their total patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would that be admissions, full admissions to hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Admissions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And of that 4 to 5 per cent of admissions, did they give you any idea as to how many of those were civilian casualties or military, i.e. combat, soldiers who had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: They didn't tell me that. Mostly, though, they did explain to me that the casualties were front line soldiers. However, occasionally one would be brought into Pale, a woman or a civilian male would be brought in from Grbavica or somewhere else around the city, but it was very low. And I did see a very few number of civilian patients in those hospitals. They were wounded by artillery or gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may return to the hospitals within Sarajevo. Regarding your visits to Kosevo Hospital, could you see at the end of 1992 and in the winter through to 1993, to start with, did you see any signs of damage from war or damage of that type to the Kosevo hospital complex?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. One day when I was there two shells did damage to two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell me, sir, when it was that you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: It was October.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: 1992. I was meeting with Medecins Sans Frontieres

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where were you when these shells landed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I was in a building near the entrance gate, south entrance gate to Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what was it you witnessed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: We heard the explosions, several people took cover in the building I was in, went down one floor because it was partially covered by ground on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: By explosions, Mr. Ashton, I presume you mean --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Artillery impact, artillery rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, would you go on, please, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I ran out towards the main hospital, and when I came out I saw people coming out of a building, one building, running towards the main hospital as well, and they said their building had just been hit, which was down the hill towards the Lion's Cemetery, the lowest building on the complex. And then I found out that one section of the main hospital had been hit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware on that occasion or did you witness on that occasion any casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Not that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are there any further occasions that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: In front of the State Hospital there was a medical staff personnel wounded outside when we were taking in patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. That happened in early 1993. I don't know the month or the day. It was around March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what was the cause of that injury to that medical staff member?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The cause or the extent?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The cause, to start with.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The cause was shrapnel hitting directly in the front up above the fifth floor of the hospital, in the front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And yes, you can describe briefly the injury to the staff member.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Wounded in the arm and the leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Returning to -- I believe we were going to see if there was a further matter -- yes. I had asked you, in fact, any other further occasions that you witnessed. By that I'm also thinking of Kosevo hospital. Did you witness any other shelling incident or other sort of firing at the Kosevo hospital, again this similar period to the early 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Yes. There were other times when shells hit when I was in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give us just an indication of the dates when you were there when such things happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Middle of 1994 I was -- late 1993 there were several incidents in which the Kosevo compound came under fire directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You're positive, late 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Because I got a complaint from a doctor when I was down at the UN headquarters. I answered the phoned in UNHCR, and he wanted to file a complaint with UNPROFOR and he said the French wouldn't answer the phone, wouldn't take his call. He was looking for Tony Land, and complained that the hospital was being deliberately shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, taking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Taking those two incidents you've now described, or at least that have occurred, could you say whether you were able to ascertain the source of the fire for the shells that struck the hospital on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: The source of fire from the first incident was only according to the people who were outside at the time the shells landed. I talked to somebody in front of the morgue next to the main hospital who said he witnessed the shell fire. He said it came from above the zoo in the Serb position up there that faced the hospital and faced down into the valley of the Lion's Cemetery in the centre of Sarajevo, but I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On the first occasion you've described, can you tell us what sort of shell it was? I mean, was this artillery tank, mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: I couldn't tell because I was inside the building when it happened, but it was a very, very large explosion. I assume it was artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And the second incident that you've mentioned at Kosevo Hospital, again, can you give any indication as to the style of ordnance that was used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Mortar rounds were used in that because they were smaller and you could hear those come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, then, you've had experience of these things. May I ask you: What is it that you hear that tells you that this is a mortar round as opposed to some other?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: Mortars and artillery are distinctively different when you're on the receiving end. Mortar makes a sound of a thump when it's fired. A propellant is faced upwards and the shell trajectory is up and then it drops down. So when the mortar round comes in, if you're within 50 yards, you will hear what sounds like a pop bottle or a pop can opening. There's a zip and then the impact almost instantaneously after the zip sound. Artillery is a loud boom and it takes a longer time to -- for the projectile to come forward. By the time the projectile reaches 1.000 metres it begins sending out a sound field, which is the whistling sound that can be observed as the shell comes in. Usually two to three seconds before the shell hits you'll hear it whistling and sometimes as much as 9 seconds, depending on how far back it is, 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Chairman, it is my impression that expert questions are going asked. I don't know if the gentleman here is an expert, whether he is an expert or not, but I feel we're going a bit too far with this detailed description.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I of course already in that sense we have gone into the background of Mr. Ashton's -- his -- I think -- he is not being held out as an expert but he is an informed observer of things and he has been personally involved. This gentleman speaks from personal experience. And if he has been exposed to certain things, where certain sounds happen or certain events take place, I would suggest to that extent he is able to offer this information. He doesn't speak as a ballistics expert; he speaks as a man whose been beneath mortars and shells.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON
utterances.text: In reference to that, I have a lot of experience with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please. It's up to the parties to discuss whether the objection is to be sustained or to be denied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied, but -- and I'll explain to you why, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The witness has given answers to the question whether certain projectiles were mortar or artillery projectiles. He was then asked to explain how he could make the difference. But the Chamber does agree with you that we are coming, although these are still matters of facts in explaining why he could give the answers he has given, that we come close to the limit of where it would become expertise. I think it's a couple of minutes after 7.00, Mr. Blaxill. I don't know whether -- there has been an intervention anyhow, if you say you have still got one or two questions, then looking at the interpreters' booth, we might continue for one or two seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have probably only a couple of questions on this, because as I say, this man is not being held as an expert witness, so just a couple of things as to his -- to the number of times he has heard such a sound or something of that order. But if you want to break now, Your Honours, we are past 7.00. I mean, I am quite content to wrap this one up in the morning, if that suits you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's better. It's almost 5 minutes over 7.00. I think we have to stop now and have a break until tomorrow morning at 9.30 and then we'll resume.
